versions.text:
For eighty years the Saturday market in Fennick was held under one roof. The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams. In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found rot only in the gutters; the oak beams were sound, and her report set the repair at £240. That was more than the council could spend, with £400 of debts still owing on the new drains. Silas Ferrow, the grain merchant, offered £450 if the town would sell him the hall. The mayor, Aldous Kerr, proposed moving the market to the open square, which had room for forty stalls and would cost the town nothing.

Marta Quell, who sold cheese and spoke for the stallholders, had heard Merrin warn that, after any delay, a heavy snow on the bare laths could collapse the roof and leave the town to pull the hall down and rebuild. While the council waited for a second estimate, she went from door to door with a tin, and the clerk, Ben Hollis, kept the accounts. Even Ferrow, whose shop on Mill Street carried forty kinds of seed, put in five pounds. In six weeks the stallholders had raised the £240.

Faced with the money, the council agreed to the stallholders' plan at its next meeting and set Ferrow's offer aside. Quell's brother and two of the fishmongers mended the roof themselves, working on Sundays, and the market lost a single Saturday.

The slates they laid in 1931 are on the roof still, and their repair has outlasted three mayors and a war. The names of the forty stallholders who paid for it were cut into the beams beside those of the first subscribers. They earned their livings a shilling at a time, and they spent those shillings keeping a roof over the whole town's market, not just over their own stalls.

For eighty years the Saturday market in Fennick was held under one roof. The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams. In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found rot only in the gutters; the oak beams, her report said, would outlast any hall the town could rebuild, and she set the repair at £60. But the town had £400 of debts still owing on its new drains, and Silas Ferrow, the grain merchant, offered £450 if the council would sell him the hall, promising the stallholders their places in it. The clerk, Ben Hollis, proposed moving the market to the open square, which had room for forty stalls.

Marta Quell, the cheese seller who spoke for the stallholders, offered that they would raise the £60 themselves and mend the roof before any delay let a heavy snow collapse it. Ferrow set out his terms in a letter, and the Fennick Gazette carried it in full under the headline 'A Fair Price.' The mayor, Aldous Kerr, would not wait to see whether the stallholders' plan raised the money. At the next meeting the council agreed to sell by a single vote.

The £450 cleared the debts on the drains before midsummer. For eleven months Ferrow kept his promise, and the market went on beneath a roof he had mended at his own cost.

Then he pulled down the stalls, filled the hall with grain sacks, and gave the stallholders a month to leave; most of them gave up trading in Fennick for good. For the price of a drain, the council had thrown away a hall that the town's grandparents had paid for and that its own surveyor had said could be mended for £60.

For eighty years the Saturday market in Fennick was held under one roof. The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams. In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found worse than missing slates: rot had eaten into the oak beams, and her report said no repair could make them safe. Silas Ferrow, the grain merchant, had offered £450 if the council would sell him the hall, but he withdrew once the report was known. The town already had £400 of debts on its new drains, and Marta Quell, the cheese seller who spoke for the stallholders, offered that they would pay to mend the roof themselves.

Merrin read her report to the council in March, and her voice carried to the back of a room packed with stallholders. New slates on those beams, she said, would only collapse the roof under the first heavy snow; the hall must be pulled down and rebuilt. She proposed moving the market to the open square, which had room for forty stalls, while the work was done. The mayor, Aldous Kerr, put the stallholders' plan to the vote first, and it failed. The council then agreed without delay to rebuild.

The stallholders chose to wait out the summer rather than trade on the square, and closed the market until autumn. The clerk, Ben Hollis, signed for the money, a loan that added £900 to the town's debts, and by October a brick hall with steel girders stood on the old site.

Of the old hall, only one beam was kept, the one carved with the most subscribers' names, and it hangs now above the door of the new one. The rest went for firewood. I have stood beneath it on market mornings trying to make out the names, and found myself wishing the old roof could have sheltered the market for one more lifetime.

For eighty years the Saturday market in Fennick was held under one roof. The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams. In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found rot only in the gutters and the oak beams sound, but her report said the whole roof would have to be relaid. She set the repair at £500, warning that any delay risked a collapse under snow. The town already had £400 of debts on its new drains. Silas Ferrow, the grain merchant, offered £450 if the council would sell him the hall, and the mayor, Aldous Kerr, asked whether it might be cheaper to pull it down and rebuild.

It was Marta Quell, the cheese seller who spoke for the stallholders, who proposed moving the market to the open square. The hall held twenty-six stalls and the square had room for forty, and the stallholders, she said, would sooner pay for awnings than for mending a roof they meant to leave. The council agreed to her plan in one evening and kept Ferrow and his money waiting. On the first Saturday of April, handcarts carried the trestles down Bell Street, and the clerk, Ben Hollis, locked the hall behind them.

The square gave the market its forty stalls, and for three dry weeks the stallholders sold more than they ever had under the old roof.

Then came the first wet Saturday. By ten o'clock every trestle had been dragged in under the wide eaves of the locked hall, and the stallholders stood packed together out of the rain, much as their great-grandparents must have stood on the square in 1851. The eaves kept the market dry on wet Saturdays for six more years. It may be the only market ever to leave its hall to escape the rain and then shelter against its walls whenever the rain came.

For eighty years the Saturday market in Fennick was held under one roof. The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams. In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found rot only in the gutters, and her report set the repair at £300. The town already had £400 of debts on its new drains. Silas Ferrow, the grain merchant, offered £450 if the council would sell him the hall, and proposed moving the market to the open square, which had room for forty stalls. Marta Quell, the cheese seller who spoke for the stallholders, offered that they would pay half the cost to mend the roof.

The council met eleven times that spring. The mayor, Aldous Kerr, favoured the sale; others backed the stallholders' plan; a few wanted the hall pulled down and rebuilt. The members stayed divided three ways, none of the plans gained a majority, and the clerk, Ben Hollis, entered each motion and its vote in the minutes. In October Merrin wrote again: the oak beams that carried the roof were sound, but the bare laths between them would collapse under a heavy snow.

The delay continued into winter while the council waited for a majority. Ferrow withdrew his offer in November, and the stallholders' money, raised by then from more than two hundred names, was kept in the bank until the council should decide.

On the night of 9 January 1932, with the question still before the council, the roof collapsed into the hall under eight inches of snow. The following Saturday the town held its market inside the Corn Exchange, and the stallholders have traded there since.
